Morgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term capital market assumptions for the first time, predicting that its returns over the next decade could outperform those of equities, bonds, and gold. This move is regarded as a milestone in Bitcoin's acceptance on Wall Street. According to Zhitong Finance, J.P. Morgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term capital market assumptions for the first time, predicting that its returns over the next decade may outperform equities, bonds, and gold. This move is regarded as a milestone in Bitcoin's acceptance on Wall Street. However, the extreme volatility of Bitcoin may undermine its appeal on a risk-adjusted basis. J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s baseline scenario projects an annualized return of 10% for Bitcoin over the next ten years, while assuming an annualized volatility as high as 55%, more than three times that of U.S. large-cap stocks. The firm stated in its report this week that Bitcoin has not yet been incorporated into its primary portfolio models due to its unstable correlation with other assets. High volatility erodes compounded returns, as significant losses require disproportionately larger gains to break even. Bitcoin ETF investors are well acquainted with this dynamic: those who bought near the peak of slightly above $126,000 in 2025 saw their positions lose up to 50% as prices retreated. The J.P. Morgan Asset Management team, including Tim Lintern, Thushka Maharaj, and Sean Daly, wrote: “We believe it is premature to view Bitcoin as a diversification tool within a balanced portfolio at this stage. However, the situation could change in the future if volatility continues to decline and correlations with other assets stabilize, particularly as regulatory clarity improves and liquidity and price discovery mechanisms continue to enhance.” Since the pandemic, numerous Wall Street institutions have increased their exposure to the cryptocurrency sector, shifting from cautious inquiry to more substantive experimentation. These efforts include offering trading services for certain cryptocurrencies, launching crypto-themed funds, and exploring tokenization. Analysts at J.P. Morgan Asset Management noted that while many investors still regard Bitcoin as a speculative asset, they continue to explore cryptocurrencies. Recent surveys indicate that one in ten clients holds cryptocurrencies in their portfolios, and approximately 17% of clients plan to “prioritize cryptocurrency allocations.” This trend is partly driven by a more mature and clear regulatory framework. Nevertheless, researchers at the firm maintain that Bitcoin is not yet sufficient to serve as a diversification tool in a balanced portfolio due to its “unstable correlation” with other assets. They wrote: “If correlations stabilize and volatility declines, the portfolio utility of Bitcoin may improve in the future.” More broadly, the report examines how “economic nationalism, technology adoption, and capital reallocation” may drive asset returns over the next decade. The authors conclude that government investments in “national resilience” and corporate competition to deploy new innovations will influence capital allocation patterns. They suggest that a $15 trillion “global capital expenditure supernova” will propel growth and robust asset returns. Bitcoin just earned a spot in one of Wall Street's most closely watched return forecasts, and it landed at the top of the table. J.P. Morgan Asset Management projected a 10% compound annual return for Bitcoin over the next 10 to 15 years in its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, released Monday. It's the 31st annual edition of the report and the first to include Bitcoin. The forecast tops the firm's projections for U.S. large-cap stocks at 7.5%, gold at 5.5% and a classic 60/40 stock-bond portfolio at 7%. The catch is volatility. The report pegs Bitcoin's annualized volatility at 55%, compared with about 17% for gold. That's why Bitcoin's arithmetic average return, a simple average of yearly gains, comes in at 20.9%, more than double the compound figure investors would actually keep after big price swings. The firm stopped short of adding Bitcoin to the models it uses to map how assets move together. "For the first time, we put a range on bitcoin returns, though we do not yet include bitcoin in our main covariance matrices," the report says. Instead, JPMorgan built a separate, smaller matrix comparing Bitcoin with a subset of assets, citing the cryptocurrency's volatility and unstable correlations as obstacles to widespread portfolio inclusion. JPMorgan also pushed back on a popular bull case, calling the idea that currency debasement will spark a rush into crypto "wide of the mark." Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan welcomed the forecast, if not every input. "First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight at you, then they add you to their Long-Term Capital Markets Assumptions paper and predict you'll be the best-performing asset of the next decade," he wrote on X. Hougan argued that JPMorgan's 55% volatility assumption is too high, which in turn makes its return forecast too conservative. Bitwise, which manages crypto index funds and ETFs, has a stake in that view. The forecast comes as JPMorgan deepens its own blockchain bets. The bank is bringing JPM Coin, a token representing dollar deposits, to Ethereum, and has joined BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and the DTCC in tokenized stock efforts. JPMorgan's JPM Coin Arrives on Ethereum, Putting Bank Dollars on a Public Blockchain The timing is notable. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs drew $526.7 million on Monday, their best day since Sept. 22, with BlackRock's IBIT taking in $665.2 million. That trimmed October's net outflows to about $88 million. Bitcoin hovered around $82,000, while the 10-year Treasury yield held above 5%, a competing return with far less volatility. JPMorgan's own global bond forecasts are their highest in two decades. title: J.P. Morgan Expands JPM Coin to Ethereum as Banks Test Tokenized Finance - TOKENPOST
content: The dollar deposit token was already available on Base. In a separate workflow, Citadel Securities used a Treasury note as collateral for overnight financing after its tokenized representation settled on BNY’s ledger. J.P. Morgan made JPM Coin available to institutional clients on Ethereum on Oct. 19, expanding the dollar deposit token beyond Base as banks develop ways to use digital assets in settlement and financing. The Ethereum rollout gives institutional clients another network for JPM Coin. It is separate from a BNY-Citadel Securities Treasury repo workflow that connected tokenized settlement to overnight borrowing. In the workflow announced Oct. 13, Citadel bought a two-year U.S. Treasury note through BNY using Tradeweb. BNY recorded a tokenized representation of the note on its private digital ledger, where the representation settled within minutes. Citadel then used the note as collateral in an overnight triparty repurchase agreement, with BNY providing cash. A repurchase agreement, or repo, is short-term financing backed by securities. In a triparty repo, a third party manages collateral and settlement between the borrower and lender. The BNY workflow carried a Treasury purchase through digital settlement and into that financing process. “BNY’s transaction is an important example of how tokenisation can improve the way securities are used in financial markets,” Brickken CEO and co-founder Edwin Mata said. The distinction between the Treasury note and its digital representation matters. The representation settled on BNY’s ledger; the underlying note did not itself settle there. Federal securities laws continue to apply to securities in tokenized form. The two bank efforts address different parts of institutional finance. J.P. Morgan’s expansion concerns access to a dollar deposit token, while the BNY transaction used a Treasury security to secure overnight cash. Both involve institutional clients, but the assets and workflows differ. Deutsche Bank is targeting a European launch of digital-asset custody for institutional and corporate clients this year, subject to its regulatory timeline. The planned service would initially support Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and selected stablecoins. Tokenized financial instruments are on the bank’s product roadmap. title: JP Morgan and SIFMA flag gaps in SEC tokenized stock exemption - Ledger Insights
content: The topic of the SEC Innovation Exemption for tokenized securities venues (TSVs) came up during SIFMA’s annual conference today. JP Morgan’s Eddie Wen asked if issuers have a right to say how their shares are represented and traded on tokenized platforms, and warned that liquidity tends to migrate toward channels with the fewest rules. Separately, SIFMA filed a comment letter on the SEC’s Innovation Exemption that puts detail behind both questions. Its two sharpest concerns are that issuers get one narrow chance to block a third party token of their stock, and that the trading volume caps apply per venue while anyone can open one. The letter lands as the framework is already in motion. Two venues have published formal notices and could begin trading within weeks, and 16 issuers have already objected to one of them. The exemption took effect on publication on September 17 without prior comment. On the issuer side it asks for a longer objection window, a named contact at the issuer, and a right to object after the initial period closes. On volume it asks the SEC to monitor aggregate trading across all venues and publish the numbers by stock. SIFMA says it understands the Commission intends to publish a list of TSVs on its website. title: JPMorgan Says One Big Headwind for Stocks May Be Fading - TradingView
content: JPMorgan JPM says the stock-market recovery could extend into year-end if global bond yields begin to stabilize, potentially easing the valuation pressure that has weighed on equities in recent months. Strategist Mislav Matejka argued that the recent surge in the 10-year Treasury yield may have gone too far. The U.S. 10-year yield crossed 5% in late September and peaked around 5.3%, its highest level in roughly two decades. JPMorgan said changes in fed funds futures explain nearly all of this year's increase in long-term yields. With much of that short-rate repricing now potentially complete, the bank sees less room for another major leg higher. That matters because rising yields have already done significant damage to stock valuations. During the sharpest phase of the selloff, 12-month forward P/E multiples for both the S&P 500 and MSCI AC World compressed by around three turns. The S&P 500 now trades at about 19.1 times forward earnings, down from 21.7 times at the start of the year. If yields stabilize, JPMorgan believes that valuation compression may not need to continue. So far, 78% of U.S. companies and 60% of European companies reporting third-quarter results have beaten consensus EPS expectations. JPMorgan also noted that the share of global companies delivering accelerating earnings growth is near record highs. I think JPMorgan's call boils down to one thing: stocks may not need falling yields to rally they may simply need yields to stop rising. Higher bond yields have pressured equity multiples, made AI infrastructure financing more expensive and tightened conditions for consumers. A more stable rate backdrop could ease all three pressures and potentially allow the rally to broaden beyond mega-cap technology stocks. For investors, the key things to watch are the 10-year Treasury yield, Fed expectations, earnings revisions and whether market breadth improves outside the largest tech names. If yields hold near current levels and earnings continue to beat expectations, the biggest valuation headwind of the past few months may finally start fading. title: JPMorgan Brings JPM Coin to Ethereum as Wall Street Embrace Expands - Cryptonews.net
content: The largest U.S. bank announced Monday that JPM Coin, which represents U.S. dollar deposits held at JPMorgan, will become available to institutional clients on Ethereum. The move follows the token’s launch on Coinbase’s Base—an Ethereum Layer 2 scaling network—in November 2025 and marks another step in the bank’s efforts to modernize payments and settlement using blockchain technology. JPM Coin enables participating clients to transfer funds around the clock, with transactions settling in seconds rather than taking days through conventional banking infrastructure. According to Bloomberg, JPMorgan expects demand from large cryptocurrency companies seeking blockchain-based payment solutions, along with financial institutions requiring digital cash to settle transactions involving tokenized assets or provide collateral. Emma Landriault, global head of Kinexys Labs at JPMorgan’s blockchain division, told Bloomberg that the expansion reflects growing convergence between traditional financial institutions and cryptocurrency companies. “We’ve clearly been in a year of further convergence between Wall Street and crypto,” Landriault said, describing increasing collaboration between established banks and institutional blockchain businesses. The bank selected Ethereum because of its substantial liquidity and existing adoption among institutional clients, Landriault said. Ethereum remains the largest decentralized finance blockchain by total value locked, with nearly $50 billion deposited in applications operating on the network, according to DefiLlama. Although JPM Coin will operate on public blockchain infrastructure, access to the deposit token will remain restricted to eligible institutional participants. Unlike conventional stablecoins, which are typically backed by reserves of cash and other liquid assets, deposit tokens represent claims on deposits held at the issuing bank. The expansion comes as major financial companies accelerate efforts to tokenize traditional assets, including stocks, bonds, and investment funds. Blockchain-based settlement could allow financial institutions to move money and securities more efficiently while reducing reliance on traditional payment systems and their operating hours. JPMorgan has emerged as one of the banking industry’s most active blockchain developers. Its Kinexys Blockchain Deposit Account network already facilitates transfers involving dollars, euros, pounds, and other currencies through the bank’s private blockchain infrastructure. That network currently processes more than $7 billion in transactions daily, according to JPMorgan. However, that figure remains relatively small compared with the approximately $12 trillion in daily payment volume handled by the bank’s broader payments business. By extending JPM Coin to Ethereum after its earlier Base deployment, JPMorgan is positioning its deposit token to serve financial institutions operating across both traditional banking systems and public blockchain networks.

Although progress has been made in yield rates and onboarding new customers, the scale remains small; it will require securing anchor customers and validating the economics of cutting-edge process nodes to become a valuation anchor. The offering is powered by 55ip’s ActiveTax Technology and builds on the company’s existing capabilities spanning model portfolios, SMAs, and direct indexing. The initial offering includes model portfolios with SMAs from J.P. Morgan Asset Management, 55ip’s parent company, and BlackRock, an established 55ip model partner. The platform’s single-account structure can combine ETFs, mutual funds, and an active SMA using either an asset manager-provided model or an advisor-provided strategy. 55ip said this approach is designed to simplify operations while giving advisors more flexibility in constructing personalized portfolios. Advisors will also receive portfolio visibility through the 55ip Portal, which will provide detailed information covering both the model and SMA components of the UMA. ActiveTax Technology will support tax-aware transitions and ongoing account management across the combined portfolio. 55ip said the expanded offering is intended to help RIAs address scalability challenges as they acquire new clients and manage increasingly complex portfolios. The structure is also designed to provide clients with direct ownership benefits associated with SMAs, including opportunities for tax-loss harvesting, while preserving the consistency and scalability offered by model portfolios. The announcement follows 55ip’s previously announced work with InvestCloud on a future UMA offering that is expected to incorporate private investments for RIAs. 55ip is a wholly owned subsidiary of J.P. title: JPMorgan sees 10% annual bitcoin returns, topping stocks, bonds and gold over next decade - CoinDesk

JPMorgan’s (JPM) asset management division expects bitcoin BTC$82,750.73 to outperform U.S. stocks, bonds and gold over the next 10 years. The asset manager forecasted a base case of 10% annualized returns for bitcoin over the next 10 years in its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report on Tuesday. The bank also set a bear case of -9.7% and a bull case of 17%. The figure compared to projected 5.6%-6.6% growth in U.S. bonds, 7.5% and 7.7% in U.S. large and small-cap equities respectively and 5.5% in gold. The report marks the first time JPMorgan has put a range on bitcoin returns in its research. The New York based banking group has a complicated history with cryptocurrency, largely due to the association of CEO Jamie Dimon’s widely publicized views of bitcoin. Dimon famously described the world’s largest crypto as a “fraud” in 2017, a skeptical position he has reiterated with somewhat softer verbiage in recent years. JPMorgan Asset Management maintained a cautious view of bitcoin in Tuesday’s report, saying its “volatility and unstable correlation to other asset classes…remain an obstacle to [its] widespread inclusion in portfolios.” Furthermore, JPMorgan does not make a case for bitcoin as a portfolio diversifier, instead viewing it as a “speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing,” according to comments by portfolio manager Dr Sheena Shah and head of digital asset strategy Dennis Cristallo. “It lacks a strategic role in portfolios other than as a bet on fiat currency expansion or future asset trading on blockchains,” they added. “BTC mostly trades like a high beta risk asset that tracks global money supply growth, but it is sometimes treated as ‘digital gold.’ Unstable correlations with other assets present a modeling hurdle. title: JPMorgan Expects Bitcoin to Beat Stocks and Gold: But There’s a Catch - CryptoPotato
content: JPMorgan Asset Management has included bitcoin in its long-term capital-market assumptions for the first time, predicting a 10% annual compounded return over the next 10 to 15 years. Nevertheless, the bank’s analysts still warned about the cryptocurrency’s extreme volatility and unstable correlations. It’s obvious that we are far from the days when JPMorgan’s CEO, Jamie Dimon, used to bash the leading cryptocurrency at every opportunity he had. The report is designed for strategic portfolio planning rather than short-term trading. In its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, JPM included a formal return forecast for bitcoin for the first time in the report’s over 30-year history. title: JPMorgan Expects Bitcoin to Beat Stocks and Gold Over the Next Decade. Why Is Justin Sun Turning More Bearish? - 24/7 Wall St.
content: JPMorgan just gave Bitcoin its first-ever spot in a long-term return forecast, while a prominent crypto founder warns that AI could shatter its security within 18 months. The two camps are making opposite bets on the same clock. J.P. Morgan Asset Management, part of JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM | JPM Price Prediction), has included Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) in its long-term return forecasts for the first time. In its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, the bank forecasts that Bitcoin could deliver a 10% compound annual return over the next 10 to 15 years, outperforming U.S. large-cap stocks at 7.5%, U.S. REITs at 8.2%, and gold at 5.5%. The report estimates Bitcoin’s arithmetic annual return at 20.9%, which is the average of its yearly gains and losses. However, because significant losses reduce savings, the compound annual return is lower, with a forecast of 10%. Bitcoin’s annual volatility is projected at 55%, indicating how much its price can fluctuate in a typical year. In contrast, Justin Sun, the founder of Tron (CRYPTO: TRX), has adopted a more cautious stance. In an interview with William Joy published October 16, 2026, Sun said advancements in AI algorithms and quantum computing could threaten Bitcoin’s security, making him “slightly more bearish.” He argued that many ETF holders and others in the industry have not fully recognized these potential threats. As of October 20, Bitcoin is priced at $81,453, having dropped 1.1% in the last 24 hours, 1.9% over the past week, and 6.8% year-to-date. This raises the question: should Bitcoin investors focus more on JPMorgan’s optimistic forecast or Sun’s warnings? JPMorgan’s long-term capital market assumptions estimate potential returns for various investments. These estimates help financial advisors and pension funds decide how to allocate capital among different asset classes. Although these estimates now include Bitcoin, JPMorgan has cautioned that it has not yet integrated Bitcoin into its primary covariance matrices, which determine portfolio allocations. The report does not introduce a Bitcoin-focused investment product or allocate resources for Bitcoin purchases. Instead, it serves as a research reference for financial advisors discussing Bitcoin with their clients. Based on JPMorgan’s compound return estimate, a $10,000 investment in Bitcoin could grow to approximately $25,937 over a decade. While this forecast offers hope, it is speculative, and the projected 55% annual volatility means investors should be wary of possible declines. Sun’s concerns extend beyond typical fears about quantum computing. He argues that advances in AI, combined with standard computing capabilities, may undermine current cryptographic security before quantum technology becomes widespread. He estimated that this risk could materialize within 1 to 1.5 years, potentially exposing unprotected wallets or private keys. Sun also criticized major financial institutions like BlackRock (NYSE: BLK) for holding substantial amounts of Bitcoin without fully understanding the risks associated with quantum computing, suggesting this lack of awareness may lead to market mispricing. His concerns merit attention, especially since many Bitcoin holdings are stuck in older wallets whose users have lost their keys, leaving them vulnerable if an attack occurs. However, Sun has his own interests. As the founder of Tron, which competes directly with Bitcoin, and as an advisor for the HTX exchange, his bearish perspective may be influenced by his competition with Bitcoin. Many cryptographers believe that the threat posed by classical computers is being overstated. Bitcoin’s security relies on elliptic-curve cryptography, which experts say conventional computers are unlikely to break within any realistic timeframe. Although Sun mentioned discussions about OpenAI’s mathematical advances, he did not provide evidence of any specific, actionable threat. In fact, Bitcoin developers are actively working to address potential quantum risks. A proposal known as BIP 360, which aims to create quantum-resistant address types, was added to Bitcoin’s improvement proposal repository in February 2026. Its authors are exploring options to implement post-quantum signatures, suggesting that while they consider the risks, significant upgrades take time and require broad agreement within the developer community. Market sentiment suggests ETF investors are unfazed by the perceived risks. On October 16—the day of Sun’s interview— U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw a net outflow of $ 82.4 million, but investors quickly turned around, adding $526.6 million on October 19, bringing total net assets to $105.5 billion. These flows do not conclusively prove holders have priced in quantum risk, but they suggest no urgent sell-off. Both headlines seem mostly like noise for Bitcoin’s near-term price. JPMorgan’s forecast gives Bitcoin a line in a planning spreadsheet, but that only becomes buying if advisers move money, and JPMorgan’s own models cannot recommend a Bitcoin allocation until the coin joins the main covariance matrices. Likewise, Sun’s warning only hurts Bitcoin if someone demonstrates a working attack. Both views are timing claims in opposite directions. JPMorgan looks 10 to 15 years out and assumes Bitcoin’s security holds, while Sun set his claim’s deadline at 12 to 18 months. If coins in old, inactive addresses start moving without explanation inside that window, his bearish view gains hard evidence. If the window passes quietly and a future report adds Bitcoin to JPMorgan’s main covariance matrices, the bullish forecast becomes something portfolios can act on. title: The new oil crisis runs through diesel - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Filling up a pickup truck with diesel right now costs about $6.50 per gallon in the United States—down a few cents from the record set in September, but still about 70% higher than in February. The most obvious explanation is the war with Iran and the crippling of the Strait of Hormuz. Crude oil was nearly $95 per barrel at publishing time, but that’s not high enough to account for the skyrocketing cost of diesel. Historically, diesel at these levels would point to crude in the $160/bbl range.1 Another way to look at it is through crack spreads, the difference between crude prices and the price of refined products.2 This measure has remained near all-time highs. Crude oil has limited economic use until a refinery turns it into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel or other products, and the global refining system is under severe strain. Global refinery throughput is running near 78 million barrels per day (bpd) in Q2, roughly 6 million bpd below the seasonal median and almost 8 million bpd lower than a year ago.3 The shortfall is concentrated in Russia, Asia and the Middle East. Russian refinery runs have fallen to 3.3 million barrels per day, down 34% year over year, while Middle Eastern refinery throughput is below 7 million bpd, down 23% year over year..4 China has not been able to offset these losses; recently, Chinese suspended product exports, adding another constraint to global supply. At the same time, global refinery outages remain highly elevated, with industry estimates of more than 9 million barrels per day of planned and unplanned downtime, roughly 4 million barrels per day above historical norms.5 The result is a refining system that is struggling to respond even as product margins remain exceptionally high. Oil is still being extracted and exported from the Middle East, but the infrastructure that turns it into a useful product and ships it is in short supply. This is visible around the world, where price signals, and government policies, highlight the shortage of refining capacity. Restoring global supply of refined product is not as simple as reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Refinery capacity has been physically destroyed in Ukraine and Russia as a result of the war, and the Middle East conflict has also damaged regional refining infrastructure around the Persian Gulf. This has compounded to strain a sector that was already running at or near max capacity following years of under-investment and global refinery closures. Global fragmentation—visible in an increased number of conflicts and a focus on energy security—has created a very tight market unable to respond to shocks. A normalization of flows through the Strait of Hormuz would undoubtedly help, but volatility in refined products could persist for some time. Higher refined fuel prices have a direct impact on growth and inflation. That’s because gasoline is mostly a consumer product. When its price rises, households have less to spend. Diesel, however, is mostly a business input: It moves freight, runs construction equipment and powers tractors, combines and garbage trucks. Almost everything consumers buy has diesel embedded in its price several times over. A sustained diesel shock raises the cost of producing and delivering nearly everything, pushing up the price of goods with no obvious connection to energy, with huge potential impacts on the economy. Our “line in the sand” when it comes to hurting economic growth is not a precise threshold, but rather a practical guidepost: sustained national average diesel above $10/gallon. J.P. Morgan Private Bank estimates suggest a diesel price per gallon of $10, versus the historical average of $3–$4/gallon, could cut U.S. growth in 2027 to roughly 0%–0.5%, from a baseline of 1.5%–2.0%. That level could also send core inflation to around 3.0%–3.2%. That kind of slowdown is consistent with unemployment rising by half a percentage point to as much as a full point. If the price of diesel were to move into that $10 per gallon territory and remain there, we would expect U.S. economic activity to slow sharply, with a meaningful chance that recession becomes the base case. This is not because $10 is a magic number, but because diesel, at that level, would represent an extreme and persistent production-cost shock to the industrial sector. Such a slowdown would also create a difficult backdrop for the Federal Reserve. A normal recession lets the Fed cut rates. This would arrive as a growth shock and an inflation shock at once. We think the Fed would respond in the traditional way of cutting rates, but with inflation already above trend, the decision would not be clear-cut. It’s natural to ask, in the event a closed Strait of Hormuz became a long-term reality, why not simply work around the Strait? The answer is that bypass routes exist and they are being used, but they trade one problem for another. Oil leaving the other coast of Saudi Arabia, on the Red Sea, must pass through Bab el-Mandeb, where Houthi forces, considered Iranian proxies, have attacked ships—at an escalating pace in recent weeks—leaving ship-to-ship transfers of the coast of Oman as the best option. The spate of recent missile attacks on Saudi Arabia highlights the fragile security environment. Further escalation, particularly on oil and gas facilities, at a time when interceptors are running low poses a material risk to oil prices. Pipelines themselves are also targets. The September strike by Iranian-allied forces on the East-West line6 was a deliberate signal that Tehran and its proxies can raise the cost of oil faster than the United States and its allies can establish new export routes around the damage. Venezuela oil production is often pointed to as a potential swing factor that can improve global supply conditions, but much of the same constraints hold and the timeline for boosting production is measured in years due to the country’s dilapidated infrastructure. Likewise regarding the recent decision to allow Russian exports of diesel, this will marginally increase global supply, but not enough to have a material impact on prices. New pipeline capacity will reduce the chokepoint risk of the Strait but new capacity can take about two to five years depending on the complexity of the project. Diesel prices are off their peak, so has the worst may have passed—or it may not have. Could diesel prices rise again, possibly even further? Prices at publishing time were already impacting the transportation, manufacturing and agriculture sectors, but a move much higher would slow economic activity broadly. Near-term trends are posing a challenge, but our base case remains that a resolution can be achieved that reopens the Strait and eases pressure on prices. The twin blockades are creating economic pressure on both sides. In Iran, economic pressures are building through high inflation, currency depreciation and product shortages. For the global economy, the pressure is felt primarily through higher fuel costs but also through market variables such as higher yields and equity volatility (see chart). Government actions aimed at releasing oil from strategic reserves, export controls and energy so-called “truces” highlight that the pressure is building. Ultimately, it is in the interest of both sides to find agreement and an end to the conflict. The sticking point is that neither side will move first and surrender the leverage that got it to the table. Two earlier ceasefires, in April and June, collapsed within weeks, so the realistic expectation is not a grand settlement but something narrower and more fragile, and the possibility that it fails and the conflict escalates again. Should that occur, the problems could compound. The Strait can reopen in days, but the damage of emptied storage tanks, broken refineries and rerouted shipping could take years to repair. The world has drawn down more than 500 million barrels of stored oil since the crisis began. U.S. crude inventories, including the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, sit at lows last seen in the mid-1980s (see chart). Those stocks were the cushion that kept oil prices from spiking even further, and they must be refilled. The restocking process means that even after a resolution, rebuilding inventories would create new oil demand. Recent policy action may ease the immediate pressure but does not resolve the underlying shortage. Emergency reserve releases can put barrels into the market quickly and reduce the risk of disruptive export bans but they also draw down the very inventories that protect the economy from the next shock. In that sense, policy is buying time rather than creating supply. For investors, the key question is whether the time policy is buying will be used to restore refining output, normalize trade flows and rebuild distillate inventories. If not, temporary relief in diesel cracks could give way to a more fragile market later, with diesel once again becoming the transmission channel from geopolitics into inflation, margins and growth. The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s forecasts see Brent crude easing to around $74 per barrel next year as supply rebuilds, and Gulf production staying below pre-conflict levels until the second quarter of 2027. Futures prices are at the highest level they’ve been since the crisis started, pointing out that the market expects prices to remain well above pre-conflict levels through the end of 2027. We think prices will fall to roughly $80 by mid-year next year, if the conflict is resolved, but we acknowledge price risks are to the upside. In portfolios, the bias should be toward inflation resilience, quality companies with pricing power, and selective exposure to energy, while remaining cautious on diesel-intensive sectors such as transportation, construction and agriculture. If diesel moves toward double digits and stays there, the issue shifts from an energy shock to a recession-risk signal. October 20,  2026 Looking through the gloom of geopolitical events, the US bank's asset management arm sets out a relatively upbeat outlook for how major asset classes will perform, suggesting that adding "diversified alternatives" such as private equity can raise risk-adjusted returns. JP Morgan
  Asset Management has raised its forecast annual return for a
  US dollar 60/40 stock-bond portfolio to 7 per cent over the next
  10 to 15 years, up from 6.4 per cent in last year’s edition. The
  report helps shape how the firm and its clients think about asset
  allocation. “Return matters, but it is no longer the whole story,” Grace
  Peters, global co-head of investment strategy at JP Morgan
  Private Bank, said. “With dispersion wider than it has been
  in years, investors anchored to a disciplined strategic asset
  allocation will find this a more compelling environment than the
  headlines suggest.” For a “60/40+” portfolio, where investors put 30 per cent into
  diversified alternatives, the projected return rises to 7.5 per
  cent, with a Sharpe ratio 21 per cent higher than the plain
  60/40. Last year that figure was 6.9 per cent, with a 25 per cent
  Sharpe ratio uplift. (The Sharpe ratio measures the performance
  of an investment such as a security or portfolio compared to a
  risk-free asset, after adjusting for its risk.) (FWR has contacted JP Morgan to clarify this point about
  whether a 30 per cent move into alternative assets would change
  the split in the overall portfolio from 60/40 and will update in
  due course.) Close correlations between stocks and bonds, which have tested
  the wisdom of the 60/40 approach, make further diversification
  necessary, many in the industry have argued. A decade-plus of
  ultra-low interest rates after the 2008 financial crash hit bond
  yields and equity yields, encouraging an inflow into private
  markets because of their illiquidity premium. The Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report, now in
  its 31st edition, draws on more than 90 portfolio managers,
  economists and analysts. The assumptions cover more than 200
  assets in over 20 base currencies and underpin strategic asset
  allocation across the group, including at JP Morgan Private Bank. In its explanation about the assumptions, JPMAM said: “We center
  the 2027 edition on three forces with durable implications:
  Economic nationalism (governments’ more domestically oriented
  posture); faster diffusion of technological innovation (tech
  adoption) and the reconfiguration of how and where public and
  private funds are deployed (capital rewiring).” JPMAM said the developed world has the strongest growth outlook
  in 15 years. It expects an AI-centered investment cycle extending
  to 2040 to raise total factor productivity by 50 per cent, to 120
  basis points. That pushes its US real GDP growth forecast to 2.1
  per cent and developed world nominal growth to 4.2 per cent.
  Labor and demographic constraints still weigh on long-term
  growth, and the firm expects inflation to remain more volatile,
  citing demographics, large government deficits and geopolitics.
  It frames the outlook around three forces: economic nationalism,
  technology adoption and a shift in public and private capital
  flows driven by rising domestic investment. In equities, the US large cap forecast rises by 80 basis points
  to 7.5 per cent, on profit margins above 15 per cent, though
  elevated starting valuations and concentration remain
  risks. Global equities are projected to return 7.5 per cent in dollar
  terms, up from 7 per cent, helped by continued but slower dollar
  depreciation. Emerging market equities will fall to 7.1 per cent
  as AI and capital expenditure tailwinds normalize. Developed
  market equity projections will overtake emerging markets for the
  first time in the report’s history, the report continued. Higher real yields will lift the global aggregate bond forecast
  to 5.3 per cent, the highest in two decades and up from a low of
  2.1 per cent in 2021. US intermediate Treasuries are expected to
  return 4.6 per cent, up from 4 per cent a year ago. US investment
  grade credit is forecast at 6.1 per cent, reflecting higher
  baseline rates and heavier issuance from hyperscalers. US high
  yield will rise to 6.7 per cent from 6.1 per cent, with a
  fair value spread of 440 basis points. The largest upgrade among alternatives is for diversified hedge
  funds, raised 140 basis points to 6.7 per cent on higher alpha
  estimates and higher rates. The global core infrastructure area will rise to 7.1 per
  cent from 6.5 per cent, supported by manufacturing reshoring.
  Private equity will edge down to 9.8 per cent and US core
  real estate will slip to 8.1 per cent, while European core
  real estate rises to 7.1 per cent from 6.9 per cent. Broad
  commodities will increase to 4.8 per cent; gold is unchanged at
  5.5 per cent and timberland will dip to 6.2 per cent. The report includes a return range for bitcoin for the first time
  but does not include it as an allocation. JPMorgan has launched its JPM Coin deposit token on Ethereum, making it available to the bank’s institutional clients. The token was first introduced in November 2025 on Base, a blockchain affiliated with Coinbase. It allows clients to send and receive funds within seconds and around the clock. According to Emma Landriault, Global Head of Kinexys Labs at Kinexys, JPMorgan’s blockchain division, the bank expects two main groups of users. The first is large clients in the cryptocurrency sector that want to make blockchain payments. The second is financial institutions that need a form of digital cash to settle or collateralise transactions involving tokenised assets. Landriault said the bank chose Ethereum because of its liquidity and its existing use among JPMorgan’s clients. Data from DefiLlama shows approximately USD 50 billion deposited in applications running on the network, measured by the total value of assets locked. Tokenisation allows traditional assets such as stocks, bonds, and funds to be represented and transferred over blockchain networks. Banks have explored the technology for more than a decade, but much of that work has taken place on private networks, where access is restricted, and institutions keep tighter control over who participates. The Ethereum deployment moves JPM Coin onto public infrastructure, although limits remain on who can hold the token. This approach gives traditional financial institutions access to existing liquidity pools and developer activity in the crypto ecosystem. Landriault described the past year as one of further convergence between Wall Street and crypto. She noted that the movement runs in both directions. Traditional institutions are moving onto public chains, while institutional web3 firms are becoming more embedded in and partnering with traditional financial institutions. The official added JPM Coin’s arrival on Ethereum reflects that shift. The launch comes as banks and large financial firms look to blockchain technology to move assets faster and work around the limitations of traditional systems. In September 2026, a company backed by more than 100 corporations, including Visa, Stripe, and Mastercard, issued a US dollar-pegged stablecoin, another form of digital money. JPMorgan Asset Management's first long-term Bitcoin forecast puts its annual compounded return at 10% over 10 to 15 years, above projections for U.S. large-cap stocks, REITs, and gold. The forecast gives Bitcoin the highest modeled return among those assets. The Bitcoin estimate appears in the firm's 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, released October 19 as its 31st annual edition. The outlook covers more than 200 asset classes, and models expected returns over a 10- to 15-year horizon for strategic investment planning. JPMorgan assigns Bitcoin a 10% annual compounded return, compared with 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 8.2% for U.S. real estate investment trusts and 5.5% for gold. That puts the Bitcoin assumption 2.5 percentage points above large caps, 1.8 points above REITs, and 4.5 points above gold. 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, JPMorgan U.S. small-cap stocks carry a 7.7% projected return in the comparison circulated by Bitwise chief investment officer Matt Hougan, who highlighted the forecast. His characterization of Bitcoin as the top-performing asset is his reading of the figures; JPMorgan's published assumptions provide modeled estimates rather than a short-term market call. The new forecast also fits a broader shift in traditional finance's engagement with digital assets. JPMorgan's institutional activity around Ethereum offers another example of the bank's expanding crypto-related work. The return forecast sits alongside a substantial risk estimate. JPMorgan assigns Bitcoin 55% annualized volatility, roughly three times the approximately 18% assumption for U.S. large-cap equities and the 17.2% estimate for gold. The report also gives Bitcoin a 20.9% arithmetic average annual return. Arithmetic return is the simple average of annual results; compounded return accounts for the effect of gains and losses across multiple periods, making the 10% figure more relevant to how value accumulates over time. With volatile assets, those measures can diverge sharply: losses reduce the capital base, so later gains must work harder to recover it. A constant 10% annual growth rate would multiply an investment by about 2.59 over 10 years and 4.18 over 15 years. That difference between return potential and realized compounding is central to interpreting the forecast. Bitcoin's risk profile also intersects with wider macro conditions, including the relationship between Bitcoin and Treasury real rates, which can shape appetite for risk assets and competing stores of value. Instead, the report uses a separate, smaller matrix that examines Bitcoin alongside selected public-market assets. A covariance matrix estimates how asset returns move in relation to one another, helping portfolio managers assess diversification and combined risk. JPMorgan identifies Bitcoin's volatility and unstable correlations with conventional assets as obstacles to including it in the main framework. The forecast quantifies Bitcoin's modeled return without prescribing a fixed allocation. That separation is consequential for institutional portfolio construction: an asset can rank highly on projected return while remaining difficult to incorporate into a strategic mix when its risk relationships shift. That tension also sits alongside changing institutional allocation behavior, including periods when Bitcoin ETF outflows persist. Flows and long-horizon assumptions measure different things, but both affect how institutions assess exposure and implementation. title: JPMorgan Expands JPM Coin to Ethereum for Tokenized Transfers - PaymentsJournal
content: As an early adopter of digital assets, JPMorgan is now positioned to build on its substantial infrastructure. After bringing its USD-backed deposit token, JPM Coin (JPMD), to the Base blockchain last year, the bank is launching the institution-focused token on Ethereum. Despite the “coin” in its name, JPMD is a unit of account for tokenized deposits—not a stablecoin. It represents deposits held at JPMorgan on a public blockchain, allowing institutional clients to make on-chain payments with greater speed and efficiency. Bringing JPMD to Ethereum, one of the most established blockchains, could expand the token’s reach and potential use cases. This expansion highlights the growing distinction between stablecoins and tokenized deposits. While both represent fiat currency in digital form, stablecoins are typically issued by private companies and backed by reserves. Tokenized deposits, by contrast, represent funds held at regulated banks, a key reason major banks have increasingly favored this approach. Several leading U.S. banks, including JPMorgan Chase, are planning to launch their own bank-led tokenized deposit network. Unlike some of its peers, JPMorgan has invested in digital assets for years. At the center of its efforts is Kinexys, one of the first blockchain platforms developed by a financial institution. The platform has evolved to support a range of functions aimed at streamlining global financial services through digital assets, including bank-to-bank transfers and foreign exchange conversions. JPMorgan recently expanded Kinexys’ foreign exchange capabilities. Last year, the bank also launched its first tokenized money-market fund on Ethereum through the platform. According to the Block, Kinexys has facilitated more than $4 trillion in transactions to date, with an average daily transaction volume of $7 billion. As tokenized deposits offer institutions new ways to streamline and automate transfers, their use could continue to grow, especially among firms engaged in foreign exchange and treasury management. Integrating JPM Coin into these transactions could further expand Kinexys’ role in institutional payments and cross-border finance. content: Phil Scott and Jim Atwood are forming Latigo Peak Partners, launching with 48 employees and a presence in Florida, Washington, Massachusetts and California. An advisory duo who managed about $18.6 billion in client assets at J.P. Morgan Advisors is going independent with the launch of Latigo Peak Partners. Phil Scott and Jim Atwood founded the RIA to work with ultra-high-net-worth individuals and families. It is based in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla., with co-operational hubs in Bellevue, Wash., and Boston, as well as a field office in Los Angeles. With its launch, the firm immediately became one of the country’s largest independent wealth firms. It remains founder-owned and self-funded, without any private equity capital, and intends to follow a long-term vision rather than manage for a future transaction. Currently, SEC records list 10 registrants affiliated with the firm. In addition to the founders, 48 professionals are with Latigo Peak at its launch. According to Scott, Latigo Peak Partners’ goal is to “build a firm geared principally toward investment performance and a distinctive client experience,” and that “independence gives us the ability to take responsibility for the future of our business and make decisions based on what we believe is right for our clients over the long term.” Related:Elevation Point Stakes $750M Ex-UBS Team in Las Vegas According to SEC records, Atwood was with Merrill Lynch from 1984 to 2018, when he joined First Republic Wealth Management (which was subsequently bought by JPMorgan following the regional bank crisis spurred by Silicon Valley Bank’s collapse in 2022). At J.P. Morgan Advisors, Scott and Atwood led two wealth management practices and, over the past six years, grew their total revenue from $34 million to $130 million. The new firm follows a family capital model, employing investment performance and comprehensive planning to meet individual family needs, without requiring families to fit a predetermined institutional model. The services include assessments of individual income requirements, risk tolerance, liquidity needs and long-term objectives, and the firm will build customized portfolios with family-office-style services, including estate and wealth planning and philanthropic advice. title: $18.6 Billion J.P. Morgan Teams Led by Phil Scott, Atwood Launch RIA - AdvisorHub
content: Two top-producing J.P. Morgan Advisors teams led by Phil Scott and Jim Atwood broke away on Friday to launch their own RIA, according to an announcement. Scott and Atwood oversaw a combined $18.6 billion and generated $130 million in revenue, according to the announcement. They have self-funded the launch of Latigo Peak Partners and are the two primary owners of the RIA through a holding company, ASO Meridian Holdings, according to the announcement. The Palm Beach Gardens, Florida-based firm has 48 employees and offices in Bellevue, Washington, as well as Boston and Los Angeles. It will use Charles Schwab & Co. and BNY’s Pershing Advisor Solutions for custody and lending, according to the announcement. Two sources close to the team said that Scott and Atwood had been frustrated by the technology and bureaucracy at J.P. Morgan. They likely forfeited substantial deferred compensation and must repay unvested balances on their forgivable recruiting loans granted when they joined a predecessor. “Nothing to do with money,” one of the sources said of the team’s reasons for moving. “They were square pegs in a round hole.” The duo touted in the announcement that their combined revenue had nearly quadrupled from $34 million over the past six years. Scott and Atwood became J.P. Morgan advisors following its parent bank’s purchase of First Republic’s assets out of government receivership in 2023. The name Latigo is tied to a ski run in Beaver Creek, Colorado, and one of the sources noted their close ties to a group of senior advisors who have met regularly in the ski town, for about two decades. A J.P. Morgan spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment. Dozens of First Republic brokers left in the year following the acquisition. The brokerage unit has around 600 brokers and is a fraction of JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s wealth division. Scott and Atwood each started their careers at Merrill in 1984 and went on to rank among its top five producers. Scott had also managed the personal wealth of other advisors at Merrill as well as their clients. Latigo manages nine in-house investment strategies and participates as a separate-account manager on Schwab’s Managed Account Marketplace, according to regulatory filings. Outside RIAs and family offices will be able to hire it while maintaining their client relationships. The release did not specify how much of the $18.6 billion is subadvised. Latigo also pays accountants a flat fee or an ongoing percentage of advisory revenue for client referrals. Scott, who is registered as Walter P. Schlaepfer, joined First Republic in Bellevue in 2020 with an 11-person team that had generated around $18 million in revenue and oversaw $2.7 billion in client assets. In the past five years, Scott has made headlines over his political donations and mixed success in clearing customer complaints from his public record. Atwood joined First Republic in 2018 in Boston with a 15-person team that generated $22 million in revenue and oversaw $4.5 billion in assets. He has no disclosures or client complaints on his record. Neither remains registered as a broker with the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. The two hired Fusion Financial Partners, a recruiting firm founded by former Hightower Advisors executives, to advise them on founding the RIA. The team had joined LPL in 2019 from Ameriprise and came to Osaic through an outside recruiter.

JPMorgan(JPM), the largest U.S. bank, brought its almost year-old crypto token, JPM Coin, to Ethereum as part of a plan to expand beyond Base, the layer-2 blockchain built by Coinbase Global COIN$170.74·Market Closed. JPM Coin, which represents dollar deposits at the bank, was technically deployed on the Ethereum mainnet on Monday and is available for institutional clients’ use, the bank said in an emailed statement. The bank chose Ethereum because the blockchain offers more liquidity than rival networks and is already used by institutional clients, Emma Landriault, the head of Kinexys Labs at JPMorgan’s blockchain division Kinexys, said in an interview with Bloomberg, which reported the news earlier. “Issuing JPM Coin first on Base and now on Ethereum is a meaningful step towards providing our institutional clients with multi-chain optionality for moving wholesale money across both the web3 and traditional finance ecosystems,” she said in the emailed statement. Broadening its availability aims to serve crypto firms that want to make blockchain payments and financial firms that need a digital token to settle trades or back tokenized assets, Landriault said. Tokenization is the process of converting real-world assets and financial assets into a digital form that’s recorded and traded on a decentralized ledger. The advantage is speed, including faster settlement of trades, quick movement of money while bypassing delays and frictions involved in traditional rails. Banks have embraced tokenization, but mostly away from public networks. In the U.S., JPMorgan, Citi (C), Bank of America (BAC) and Wells Fargo (WFC), along with more than a dozen other banks, have plans to start a shared network for tokenized deposits. JPMorgan’s private blockchain network, Kinexys, already handles more than $7 billion a day, a small piece in the bank’s $12 trillion a day payments business. Almost $50 billion worth of crypto assets are locked in Ethereum-based applications, according to DeFiLlama. Abroad, JPMorgan is among more than 30 banks that are helping Swift, the interbank messaging service, define the features and governance of its blockchain-based ledger. In July, Swift said 17 banks, including Citi and Wells Fargo, were preparing to pilot live transactions on it. JPMorgan wasn’t on that list. title: US BROKER MOVES: INTC upgraded at JPM; PYPL downgraded at Cleveland Research - Newsquawk
content: Daily broker roundups of this size are routine, and history shows most single-name rating changes fade within the session unless they mark a genuine inflection in the sell-side consensus or come from a house with prior form on the name. The headline picks are instructive in different ways: a move off Underweight to Neutral at a major house on a heavily shorted, story-driven semiconductor name is the kind of capitulation upgrade that has historically mattered more for positioning than for fundamentals, since it removes a bearish anchor rather than adding a bullish one. title: JPMorgan Takes JPM Coin To Ethereum As Banks Test Public-Chain Settlement - TradingView
content: JPMorgan is taking its bank-issued deposit token onto public Ethereum, an expansion that puts an established Wall Street payments product on infrastructure traditionally associated with crypto-native finance. TL;DR: JPMorgan is expanding access to JPM Coin on Ethereum for institutional users. The token represents bank deposits rather than an independently issued stablecoin, and participation remains restricted. The significance is in who is allowed to move the money, and where. JPM Coin gives eligible customers a tokenized claim on dollars deposited with JPMorgan. Its move onto Ethereum creates a way for institutions to send funds and settle transactions around the clock while still operating inside the bank’s permissioning framework. That distinction separates deposit tokens from the conventional stablecoin model. A holder of a dollar stablecoin generally has a claim governed by the issuer’s redemption arrangements and reserve assets. JPM Coin is bank money represented in token form. It is not being offered as a freely transferable dollar for ordinary Ethereum users. JPMorgan previously introduced the deposit token on Base, and Ethereum provides another venue where financial institutions and tokenization platforms can coordinate payments. Potential uses include moving collateral and settling transactions against tokenized assets, where a conventional banking cut-off can create delay between the asset leg and the cash leg. A public blockchain does not automatically make the system open to everyone. The bank continues to control institutional access and compliance. The development is better understood as traditional finance adopting a public settlement network without abandoning its existing customer controls. For Ethereum, that may be the bigger story: a major bank choosing its infrastructure for business that depends on predictable dollar settlement, rather than simply issuing another experiment. title: Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments - CNBC
content:
JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative, the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms. The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview. Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments, has “hit the ground running,” Petno said. “He’s done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies,” he added. Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project’s mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago. He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors, in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon. The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries. “There’s a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems,” Petno said. These “early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S.” rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said. In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup’s founder. That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers. “Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term,” Combs said in a statement Monday. “Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains,” Combs said. JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor. Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago. In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank. That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine, a former co-head of investment banking. JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada. Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno. JPMorgan is also in regular communication with the U.S. Department of Defense and Department of Commerce about the government’s needs, he said. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you.
